# Document schema

The shapes pqprobe writes for machines, and what a consumer may conclude from
them. The tables below are generated from the types that render the documents,
so a field here is a field the tool emits.

Today's `schema` is **1**.

## What the number promises

`schema` moves when the **shape** moves: a field renamed or removed, an object
nested differently, an array that becomes an object. It does **not** move for:

- a new field — a parser that breaks on an unknown key was already broken;
- a new class, check, finding or profile — those are *values*, and new ones
  appear whenever the tool learns to say something new;
- a new metric family in the Prometheus textfile;
- any change to the wording of a `message`, `title`, `hint` or `summary`.
  Prose is for people: read `value`, `unit`, `status`, `check` and `class` instead.

A document that carries no `schema` at all was written before pqprobe had the
field, and is read as this schema. A document carrying a **higher** number is
refused by `--baseline`: the fields it would be read for may mean something
else.

## The `--json` document

```console
$ pqprobe probe origin.example.com --json
```

### `Document`

| Field | Type | Present | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `schema` | number | always | which document contract this is; see the number at the top of this page |
| `tool` | string | always | always `pqprobe` — a document that says anything else is not one of ours |
| `reports` | array of [`Report`](#report) | always | one entry per endpoint probed, in the order the run produced them |

### `Report`

| Field | Type | Present | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target` | string | always | the endpoint as it was probed, `host:port` (with ` (sni …)` appended when the server name differs from the host) |
| `class` | string | always | what this endpoint is, in one word — see [Findings](findings.md) for the list |
| `results` | array of [`Result`](#result) | always | one entry per client profile, in the order they were dialled |
| `findings` | array of [`Finding`](#finding) | always | every statement about this endpoint, worst first |

### `Result`

| Field | Type | Present | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `profile` | string | always | the client shape that was dialled: a capability class, never a fingerprint of a real client |
| `ok` | boolean | always | whether that shape completed a handshake |
| `kind` | string | always | how the attempt ended: `ok`, `alert`, `reset`, `timeout`, `eof`, `refused`, `not-tls`, `dns`, `proto` or `other` |
| `error` | string | when set | the error as the TLS stack reported it, when the attempt did not complete |
| `tls_version` | string | when set | the negotiated version, e.g. `TLS 1.3` |
| `group` | string | when set | the negotiated key exchange group, e.g. `X25519MLKEM768` |
| `cipher` | string | when set | the negotiated cipher suite |
| `alpn` | string | when set | the protocol agreed by ALPN, when one was |
| `elapsed_ns` | number (nanoseconds) | when set | how long the attempt took, in nanoseconds |
| `pq` | boolean | when set | true when the negotiated key exchange was a post-quantum hybrid |
| `chain` | array of [`Cert`](#cert) | when set | the certificate chain as the peer sent it, leaf first |
| `chain_verified` | boolean | always | whether that chain verifies against the system roots — verified after the handshake, never by the dialler |
| `chain_error` | string | when set | why the chain did not verify |
| `attempts` | number | when set | how many handshakes this result is based on: two when an abrupt failure was re-dialled to confirm it |
| `first_kind` | string | when set | how the first attempt ended, when there was more than one |
| `reproduced` | boolean | when set | both attempts ended abruptly: the refusal is a wall rather than a flap |
| `flapped` | boolean | when set | the first attempt ended abruptly and the second connected: the endpoint works and is unstable |
| `ech_accepted` | boolean | when set | the peer accepted Encrypted Client Hello — read from the connection, never inferred from a handshake that merely succeeded |
| `hello_bytes` | number | when set | the size on the wire of the first ClientHello record, measured rather than estimated |
| `hello_count` | number | when set | how many ClientHellos went out; two means the peer sent a HelloRetryRequest |
| `hrr` | boolean | when set | the peer answered with a HelloRetryRequest: it asked for a different group, which costs a round trip |
| `client_cert_requested` | boolean | when set | the peer asked for a client certificate: this endpoint is mutual TLS |
| `chain_bytes` | number | when set | what the whole chain cost on the wire, in bytes of DER — the headroom number for post-quantum certificates |
| `peer_chain_len` | number | when set | how many certificates the peer sent; one means it sent the leaf alone |

### `Cert`

| Field | Type | Present | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bytes` | number | when set | the DER length the peer sent for this certificate |
| `subject` | string | always | the certificate's subject common name |
| `issuer` | string | always | the issuer's common name |
| `not_after` | string (RFC 3339) | always | when the certificate expires, RFC 3339 |
| `not_before` | string (RFC 3339) | always | when the certificate becomes valid, RFC 3339 |
| `dns_names` | array of string | when set | the names the certificate is valid for |
| `is_ca` | boolean | always | whether this certificate is a CA |
| `key_bytes` | number | when set | what this certificate's subjectPublicKeyInfo weighs in the DER the peer sent — one of the two inputs to the post-quantum projection |
| `sig_bytes` | number | when set | what this certificate's signature weighs in that same DER — the other input: an ML-DSA certificate is this certificate with those two fields replaced |
| `key_alg` | string | when set | what kind of key this certificate carries — `RSA`, `ECDSA`, `Ed25519` — as `crypto/x509` names it |
| `key_bits` | number | when set | how big that key is: the modulus for RSA, the curve size for ECDSA, 256 for Ed25519; absent when this build cannot work it out, never guessed |
| `sig_alg` | string | when set | what signed this certificate, e.g. `SHA256-RSA` — recorded, not judged: whether it is good enough is a configuration opinion |

### `Finding`

| Field | Type | Present | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `check` | string | always | which statement this is — see [Findings](findings.md) for the list |
| `target` | string | always | what the statement is about: the endpoint, or `host:port/profile` for a per-profile one |
| `status` | string | always | `OK`, `WARN`, `BAD` or `ERROR` |
| `message` | string | always | the statement, in one line of prose; **never parse this** |
| `value` | number | when set | the number the statement is about, when there is one — read this rather than the message |
| `unit` | string | when set | what that number counts, e.g. `days`, `bytes` |
| `hint` | string | when set | what to do about it, naming the affected clients |

## The `--findings` array

`--findings` is the flat array — the [`Finding`](#finding) objects above and
nothing around them, worst first. An empty run emits `[]`, never `null`, so a
consumer that iterates does not have to special-case a healthy fleet.

It carries no `schema` field, because it has nowhere to carry one: the document
is an array. Its contract is the `Finding` table above, and it moves with the
same number.

## The `--findings=wrapped` document

### `WrappedDocument`

| Field | Type | Present | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `schema` | number | always | which document contract this is |
| `check` | string | always | always `pqprobe` |
| `status` | string | always | the worst severity in the run, lower-cased |
| `summary` | string | always | the one line a digest quotes when it has room for one |
| `findings` | array of [`WrappedFinding`](#wrappedfinding) | always | the findings, worst first |

### `WrappedFinding`

| Field | Type | Present | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | always | a stable fingerprint of this problem on this target — see below |
| `severity` | string | always | `ok`, `warn`, `bad` or `error`, lower-cased |
| `title` | string | always | the finding's message |
| `detail` | string | when set | the finding's hint, when it has one |
| `target` | string | always | what the finding is about |
| `check` | string | always | which statement this is |
| `value` | number | when set | the number the statement is about, when there is one |
| `unit` | string | when set | what that number counts |

### What `id` is a fingerprint of

`id` exists so an aggregator can tell a finding it has already seen from a new
one. It is the first 6 bytes of `sha256(check + "|" + target)`, hex-encoded —
the identity of the **problem**, deliberately not of the sentence describing
it. A message carries days and byte counts that change on their own, and an id
derived from the text would report a new problem every morning.

Two findings of one check on one target in a single run would otherwise share
an id, so the second and later ones are suffixed `-2`, `-3`. The suffix is
part of the id and is stable for as long as the run keeps producing them in
the same order.

An id changes when the target changes — probing `origin.example:443` by name
and by address are two identities, because they are two things that can fail
separately.

## The Prometheus textfile

`--textfile` writes these families. The file is replaced whole, so a target
that stops being probed stops having series rather than keeping stale ones.

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pqprobe_last_run_timestamp_seconds` | When pqprobe last completed a run. |
| `pqprobe_schema_version` | Which document contract this file speaks; see docs/schema.md. |
| `pqprobe_endpoints` | How many endpoints the run probed. |
| `pqprobe_class` | The endpoint's class, as a label. Always 1. |
| `pqprobe_status` | Worst finding severity: 0 OK, 1 WARN, 2 BAD, 3 ERROR. |
| `pqprobe_findings` | Findings per status. |
| `pqprobe_cert_expiry_days` | Days until the leaf certificate expires. |
| `pqprobe_handshake_ok` | Whether that client shape completed a handshake. |
| `pqprobe_hello_bytes` | Size on the wire of the ClientHello that shape sent. |

Labels are `target`, `class`, `profile` and `status`. A new label on an
existing family moves the schema; a new *value* of one does not.

## What is allowed to grow

- **Fields.** New ones appear in any of the objects above. Ignore what you do
  not know.
- **Values.** New classes, checks, kinds, profiles and groups appear as the
  tool learns to say more. Treat an unknown one as unknown rather than as an
  error, and never as `ok`.
- **Findings.** A run emits more of them over time. The number of findings is
  not a signal; their `status` is.

What will not change without the number moving: the name and nesting of every
field in the tables above, the meaning of `status` and `severity`, and what
`id` is computed from.
